short: Faster abilities bring your next turn sooner.
long: Turn order is a clock, not a queue: after acting, a unit's next turn arrives in Initiative-cost x 100 / EFFECTIVE Speed ticks - effective, so every speed change really does bend it. Every ability lists its Initiative cost (a basic action costs 2.0) - a cheap, quick ability means you act again sooner, a heavy one leaves you exposed longer. Slowed cuts speed a quarter; Chilled cuts it a quarter at one stack and a half at two or more, so a chilled enemy genuinely waits longer between turns; Quick Draw shrinks the wait. The opening roll of the battle reads effective speed too, so a fight that starts with everyone Chilled or Frenzied starts in the order that implies. Losing a turn to Stun, Freeze, or Break still pushes the clock forward a full basic action - but a Cryomancer's Glacial Hold is not a lost turn, it is removal: a held enemy leaves the bar entirely until he releases it. The bar across the top of the battle shows the coming turns; hovering an ability shows a gold ghost of where it would put your next one.

short: Stop the sweeping marker in the center for a stronger action.
long: Every action you take runs a timing check: a marker sweeps the bar (about 0.7s each way) - press SPACE or click to stop it. The gold center is PERFECT: +15% damage or healing, +25% Break damage, and many abilities add a unique bonus effect on top. The green band is Good: full normal effect. Outside both is Sloppy: only 60% damage and half the Break damage. The check never changes your chance to miss, be parried, or crit - it multiplies what lands. Your timing matters as much as your build.

short: Attacks fill a Break meter; a full meter costs the victim a turn.
long: Alongside HP damage, most attacks carry Pressure - Break damage (BD) - which fills the target's Break meter (0-100). High Constitution shrinks incoming BD proportionally; crits deal 1.5x BD. The meter never drains on its own: it keeps climbing until it fills and the unit BREAKS - losing its next turn, dropping 30% of its armor, and taking +25% crit chance against it. When the Broken turn passes, the unit recovers and its meter empties back to zero. Breaking a boss also strips its immunity to stuns and mind magic for the duration.

short: 10% base chance: 1.5x damage and 1.5x Break damage.
long: Attacks have a 10% base chance to crit for 1.5x damage and 1.5x Break damage. A Broken target takes +25% crit chance from everyone. Many talents and spec mechanics push the roll further - the Sharpshooter's Focus adds +0.5% per point up to its conversion point (past which it buys critical MULTIPLIER instead), and Resonance stacks add a flat +1% each for the Arcanist. Only a few effects raise the 1.5x multiplier itself.

short: 5% base chance for any single-target attack to whiff.
long: Single-target attacks miss 5% of the time at base. Being Dazed adds +20%, Blind adds +50%, and attacking an Elusive target adds +25%. Area attacks never miss. A miss deals nothing at all - no damage, no Break, no on-hit effects.

short: A parried hit still lands, but at a quarter strength.
long: Heroes parry incoming melee attacks 5% of the time at base (enemies 2.5%); talents, stances, and buffs raise it. A parried hit is not negated - it lands at 25% damage and 25% Break damage. Ranged attacks cannot be parried (unless a talent says otherwise), area attacks cannot be parried, and a Broken unit cannot parry at all.

short: The dead sit the fight out - but victory brings everyone back at 20%.
long: A hero at 0 HP falls: they lose every status, take no turns, and contribute nothing until raised. Mid-battle, a Revive Potion brings them back at 50% HP and the Cleric's Resurrection at 20-25%. If the party WINS the battle, the Untouched refuse to stay down: every hero - fallen or merely battered - leaves the fight with at least 20% of their max HP. Only losing everyone ends the run.

short: Loses next turn. -30% armor, +25% crit chance against this unit.
long: The Break meter filled: this unit loses its next turn, its armor drops by 30%, everyone crits it +25% more often, and it can neither Block nor parry. A Broken boss also loses its immunity to stuns and mind magic. When the lost turn passes the unit recovers and its Break meter resets to zero - the window is short, so spend it hard.

short: Loses their next turn.
long: A stunned unit skips its next turn entirely (statuses and cooldowns still tick during the skipped turn). Bosses are immune unless Broken. Sources include Pommel Strike, sprung traps, and some enemy attacks.

short: -25% speed; turns arrive later.
long: Slowed cuts speed by 25%, which pushes every coming turn later on the initiative timeline. It does not stack with itself - reapplying just refreshes the longer duration.

short: Stacking frost: slower each stack; 4 stacks freeze solid.
long: Chill stacks up to 4: one stack is -25% speed, two is -50%, three also cuts the victim's damage dealt by 15%, and the fourth FREEZES them. A new application resets the timer of the whole pile. Chill applied by a Cryomancer NEVER expires on its own, and his fourth stack is not a brief freeze but a Glacial Hold: the pile stays at 4 for as long as he holds the enemy, and drops to one lingering stack only when he releases it, so the next build starts warm.

short: Frozen solid: skips turns until the ice thaws.
long: A frozen unit loses its turns until the freeze expires (it thaws one step during each skipped turn). Freezing comes from stacking Chilled to 4. Bosses are immune unless Broken. A freeze the CRYOMANCER causes is different: it never expires at all - see Glacial Hold.

short: The Cryomancer's freeze: indefinite, and only he can end it.
long: The Cryomancer's passive. Four stacks of his Chilled put an enemy in a HOLD rather than a brief freeze: it leaves the turn order entirely and stays there INDEFINITELY. Nothing thaws it by accident - not damage from your allies, not his own Blizzard, not the passing of turns, not an enemy Cleansing Rite. It ends only when he ends it: Ice Lance on the held enemy, the Shatter capstone (which breaks every hold at once), or a new freeze past his limit, which frees the oldest. He holds ONE enemy, two with Second Prison, any number under Absolute Zero; Cryoclasm moves a hold to a different enemy without spending it. A held enemy takes +15% damage from EVERY source (+30% with Killing Frost), so the hold is a party-wide damage window as well as a lockdown. A released enemy comes back on 1 stack of Chilled. BOSSES: they resist the freeze until Broken, and a held boss shrugs the ice off after one turn.

short: Healing received reduced by 50%.
long: Frostbitten flesh knits badly: all healing this unit receives is halved while it lasts.

short: Fire damage at each turn start; reapplying extends it.
long: A burning unit takes fire damage at the start of each of its turns - about 6% of the applier's Attack, locked in when the burn lands. Burn is fire-typed: fire resists shrink the ticks and fire vulnerability feeds them. Reapplying Burn ADDS duration rather than resetting it, so a fire build can keep a target lit indefinitely.

short: Stacking nature damage at each turn start.
long: Each poison stack ticks for about 3% of the applier's Attack at the victim's turn start, plus a flat bonus per stack from Potent Toxins, and stacks have no cap - the pile grows, and each new stack refreshes the timer. Poison is nature-typed, so nature resists blunt it. The Survivalist's Venom lane makes each application CARRY a second affliction: Coated Blades adds Cripple, Distillate adds Exposed, Slow Acting adds Slowed. Some poisons (Slow Acting, Perfected Toxin) are sticky and cannot be cleansed - and a sticky poison survives a Harvest, so Harvest is not paid for it. CREEPING DEATH reads the clock: applying any status to a poisoned enemy refreshes that poison to full duration, and if the poison is PERMANENT - which is what Perfected Toxin makes it - there is no duration to refresh, so it adds a stack instead, once per enemy per turn. You cannot extend forever, so you deepen.

short: Buildup meter: at 100 the target bleeds out for 20% max HP.
long: Wounding attacks add Bleed buildup (0-100). The meter never decays - it only climbs - and at 100 the target BLEEDS OUT: an immediate 20% of its max HP, ignoring armor and dealing no Break, after which the meter resets and builds again. Berserker talents feed on bleedouts and can chain the burst to other enemies.

short: -35% armor.
long: Sundered armor protects 35% less while the status lasts. It multiplies with a Break's -30%, so a Broken, Sundered target is close to bare.

short: Must attack the taunter.
long: A mocked enemy can only aim its attacks at whoever taunted it - the Warden's Mocking Blow and the bear's Guardian's Roar both force the fight onto the party's sturdiest shoulders.

short: Takes 15% more damage.
long: An exposed unit takes 15% more damage from every source while the status lasts.

short: -25% damage dealt.
long: A crippled unit deals 25% less damage with everything until it fades.

short: Attacks are 20% more likely to miss.
long: A dazed unit's attacks miss an extra 20% of the time, on top of the 5% base.

short: Attacks are 50% more likely to miss.
long: Blinded attacks miss an extra 50% of the time - most of what this unit swings at, it will not hit.

short: Charmed: strikes its own allies, dazing them.
long: A bewitched unit turns on its own side, basic-attacking its allies and Dazing them with every strike. Bosses REFUSE it outright until they are BROKEN - the key is the Break meter, so grind it down first (the Occultist's own Broken Will and Entropy exist for exactly that job).

short: 50% each turn to act against its own side.
long: Madness: each turn there is a 50% chance the unit turns on its own - attacking a fellow, or casting its helpful magic on the enemy side. Bosses REFUSE it outright until they are BROKEN - the key is the Break meter, so grind it down first (the Occultist's own Broken Will and Entropy exist for exactly that job).

short: 10 Break damage at the start of each turn.
long: Rot eats at the will: a decaying unit takes 10 Break damage at each of its turn starts, marching its own meter toward a Break with no further help.

short: Marked 2 per debuff: +2% damage taken per stack; no cap, never clears.
long: The Occultist's debuffs mark enemies with 2 Ruin apiece, and the mark is permanent: it has NO MAXIMUM and it NEVER CLEARS, not even when it detonates. Each stack is +2% damage taken (5% with Deeper Hex), and each stack deepens the draught heroes drink when they strike it - 2% of the damage dealt per stack, capped at 40% however many stacks and talents pile up. Every TENTH stack the mark is primed and DETONATES when the victim next acts: shadow damage off the Occultist's Attack, and the party is mended by the Old Gods' feast. The stacks SURVIVE the blast, so the next one waits for the next multiple of ten - and the Avatar of Ruin capstone moves that to every fifth.

short: Next turn: strikes a fellow with double Break damage.
long: The maddened unit spends its next turn striking one of its own with DOUBLE Break damage, Sundering them in the bargain. Bosses REFUSE it outright until they are BROKEN - the key is the Break meter, so grind it down first (the Occultist's own Broken Will and Entropy exist for exactly that job).

short: Branded: half its damage taken echoes to its whole party.
long: A branded unit becomes a conduit: half of all attack damage it takes echoes out to every member of its party. Focus fire on the sigil and the whole warband pays.

short: Elemental resistances reduced.
long: The victim's resistances to non-physical schools are lowered while this holds, deepening every elemental hit against it.

short: Armor permanently burned away.
long: Armor burned away for the rest of the battle - a small permanent reduction that keeps deepening while the target burns. NOTE: nothing in the game applies this today. Batch AR re-specced the Pyromancer talent that did, and the status is kept the way a vaulted ability is kept, so a later batch can point something at it again.

short: A trap waits: next action springs a stun and poison.
long: A Survivalist trap waits underfoot: the next time this enemy acts, the trap springs - it is Stunned for a turn and Poisoned. Trap talents add crippling, bone-breaking Break damage, or wounds that refuse healing.

short: Cannot be healed.
long: The trap's teeth hold the wound open: this unit cannot be healed at all - potions, spells, and regeneration all fail while it lasts.

short: All abilities act 50% faster.
long: The Sharpshooter's Quick Draw hastens its bearer by 50% for several turns - every ability's next turn arrives sooner on the timeline. One of the boss-trophy abilities.

short: Every attack carries one damage type; resists and weaknesses key off it.
long: All damage in the game belongs to one of seven schools: Physical, Fire, Frost, Nature, Shadow, Arcane, and Holy. Each enemy resists some schools and is vulnerable to others - the same Fireball can be shrugged off by one warband and ruin another. Scouting a fight node on the map shows the warband's identity ('Resists / Soft to'); hovering a unit in battle shows its exact percentages.

short: The steel school - most weapon attacks.
long: The default school: swords, arrows, claws. Few enemies resist it outright and none are very soft to it - physical damage is reliable but rarely finds a weakness to exploit.

short: The Pyromancer's school; Burn ticks are fire-typed.
long: Fire burns twice: the hit itself, and the Burn it so often leaves behind - Burn ticks check fire resistance too. Fire is the counter the forest fears.

short: The Cryomancer's school of Chill and Freeze.
long: Frost trades raw numbers for control: its hits Chill, and stacked Chill freezes. Several ranged enemy kinds are soft to it.

short: The Survivalist's school; Poison ticks are nature-typed.
long: Venom, thorn, and rot. Poison ticks check nature resistance, so a nature-resistant enemy blunts a poison build twice - and forest wardens resist it heavily.

short: The Occultist's school of hexes and Ruin.
long: The Old Gods' school: hexes, sigils, and Ruin detonations. A good share of the wilds' brutes and shamans are soft to shadow.

short: The Arcanist's school of raw magic.
long: Raw magical force, fed by Resonance. Armored line-holders - shieldmasters and chiefs - tend to be soft to arcane where steel fails.

short: The Cleric's rare school of smites.
long: The rarest school - a handful of Cleric smites carry it. Little in the wilds resists the light.

short: Resists shrink a school's damage; vulnerabilities amplify it.
long: A resistance removes that fraction of incoming damage of its school BEFORE armor is applied - 50% frost resist halves every frost hit. A vulnerability is the same dial pushed negative: 'Vulnerable: Fire +25%' means every fire hit lands 25% harder. Armor then reduces what remains (never beyond 85%), and every hit that connects deals at least 1 damage. Warband resists are worth scouting on the map before you commit to the fight.

short: The Warrior's fuel: builds in the fight, spent on his heaviest blows.
long: Warriors start every battle at 0 Rage (cap 100) and build it by fighting: +5 at each turn start, +10 every time they are hit, and more from rage-generating attacks like Strike. Their strongest abilities spend it. A Warrior who has been in the thick of it longest hits the hardest.

short: The casters' pool: regenerates slowly, restored by rests and potions.
long: Mage, Cleric, and Hunter abilities spend Mana (cap 100). It regenerates +12 at each turn start (the Mage's Evocation nearly doubles that), and rests, potions, and victory relics refill it between fights. Unlike Rage it carries over between battles - a drained Cleric stays drained until the party recovers.

short: The Arcanist's stacks: UNCAPPED, permanent, and compounding both ways.
long: Damaging casts build Resonance - 1 per cast, 2 on a crit - and it has NO MAXIMUM. Nothing removes it either: no decay, no cap, no reset, and it persists to the end of the battle. The bonuses COMPOUND rather than scaling per stack: at N stacks the damage bonus is 1.5% x N(N+1)/2 and the damage TAKEN penalty is 0.75% x N(N+1)/2, both uncapped, plus a flat +1% crit chance per stack. So 5 stacks is +22% damage and +11% taken; 8 is +54%/+27%; 12 is +117%/+59%; 16 is +204%/+102%. That curve IS the Arcanist - nothing early, everything late: at five stacks he is weaker than a flat per-stack ramp would make him, and by twelve he has roughly doubled while taking half again as much. The only thing that removes Resonance is Stabilize, which he does not start with and has to earn - it vents everything above 2 for Mana and a short damage shield, and it is the escape hatch from the escalation.

short: The Holy cleric's stacks, earned when allies fall into danger.
long: Whenever any party member drops below half health, the Holy cleric gains a stack of Mercy (cap 5). Each held stack adds +5% to all healing done, and stacks are the fuel for Empowering casts. Mercy rewards the healer who waits for the moment of need.

short: Spend a Mercy stack to supercharge the next Holy cast.
long: The Holy cleric can arm an Empower (E in battle), spending 1 Mercy to supercharge the next Heal, Renewal, Hymn, Resurrection, or Divine Plea - Resurrection, for one, returns the fallen at FULL health. An Empowered cast forgoes its Perfect skill-check bonus; the surge replaces finesse.

short: The Devout's gift: stacks that grow on shielded allies and on holy ground.
long: Faith lives on the Devout's ALLIES, not the Devout. Two things build it: every hit a Divine Shield absorbs builds a stack on its bearer, and every ally standing on Consecrated Ground gains one at the start of their turn (cap 5). Each stack grants 3% damage reduction and +2% damage dealt. At 5 the Faith releases - a heal of 15%+ max HP - and the stacks reset to build again. Every release also makes the Devout himself a little bigger: his maximum health rises 3% for the rest of the battle and he is healed for the same amount, so the more his shields are tested, the more there is to shield with.

short: The Sharpshooter's aim: builds on one target, lost on switching.
long: Every attack on the SAME target builds +20 Focus and THE METER HAS NO CEILING; switching targets dumps it to zero, and a kill banks up to 50 toward the next mark (all of it under Overkill). THE PAYOFF CONVERTS AT 100: the first 100 points each grant +0.5% critical chance, and every point beyond 100 grants +0.5% of critical MULTIPLIER instead - so Lethal Aim's x2 becomes x2.5 at 200 Focus and x3 at 300, and it never stops paying. Patience buys certainty first, then force. Deep Focus moves that conversion point down to 60; Spray of Arrows is the one talent that still imposes a ceiling, at 50. Coup de Grace spends the whole meter but reads at most 200 points of it, and the One Shot capstone fires at 200.

short: The Beastmaster's passive: each active beast grants its own boon.
long: Every beast the Beastmaster fields grants a boon that scales with its Loyalty - Ursus draws enemy attacks and blunts what reaches the hunter, Canis sharpens him against wounded prey, Aguila lifts the whole party's crit chance. The boon is x(1 + 0.20 per Loyalty stack) and it has no ceiling. HE NORMALLY FIELDS ONE BEAST; under THE PACK capstone he fields TWO AT ONCE, each with its own Loyalty meter, and BOTH boons apply at FULL strength - a swap then replaces whichever of the two holds LESS Loyalty, so the deeper bond always keeps its place (a tie falls to the older). Menagerie keeps an absent beast's boon alive at half strength, and Vengeance carries a dead one's for the rest of the battle. Lone Bond is the opposite bargain and closes The Pack outright: one beast, arriving deep, growing twice as fast.

short: The Beastmaster's bond, built per beast, uncapped, lost with it.
long: Each living beast builds Loyalty at the hunter's turn start, and there is NO CEILING on it. Every stack is +5% companion strike damage plus that beast's own gift, and the Pack Bond boon itself climbs continuously with the meter - x(1 + 0.20 per stack), so x2 at five, x3 at ten, x5 at twenty, and it never plateaus. Exactly one talent still imposes a cap: Wild Rotation holds it at 3, and that is the price of swapping freely. A beast's death wipes its Loyalty - the bond dies with it, and that is the whole stake of the partnership. It also decides who leaves: under The Pack a third summon replaces whichever standing beast holds LESS Loyalty (a tie falls to the older), so depth is never traded away for a fresh arrival.

short: The Occultist's meter lives on the enemy, as Ruin stacks.
long: The Occultist has no bar of their own - their power accumulates on ENEMIES as stacks of Ruin - 2 for every debuff they apply - with no ceiling and no expiry. See the Ruin status for what the mark does and how it detonates.

short: Three lanes crossed by seven rows: one node per row, one capstone per hero.
long: Each spec's tree is three themed LANES crossed by seven ROWS, plus a capstone shelf underneath - 24 nodes in all, and every node costs exactly 1 point. A ROW HOLDS ONE NODE PER LANE AND YOU PICK EXACTLY ONE: the other two are barred, drawn greyed with a lock, and their tooltip names what barred them. Hovering a node dims the two it would close, and every row is drawn inside a CHOOSE ONE band, because the row is one decision rather than three picks. Row 1 is open from the start and each later row opens when the one above it has been picked, so a build can zig-zag across the lanes or run straight down one - there is no lane requirement anywhere. The capstone shelf opens once all seven rows are picked, and it is ONE CAPSTONE PER HERO, EVER, from any lane: taking one bars the other two for the rest of the run. A run pays more points than a tree has rows, and the surplus forces a SECOND node open in a row already picked; the third node in that row stays shut forever. If a node grants an ability you have already earned elsewhere, it upgrades that ability instead of granting it.

short: Nodes get pricier as you own more: 1,1,1,2,2,2,3...
long: A hero's Nth new talent node costs ceil(N/3) points, counting all lanes together: the first three nodes cost 1 each, the next three 2, and so on. Extra ranks in a node you already own always cost 1. Spreading wide stays cheap; the deep nodes of a focused build are bought at the steep end of the curve.

short: Every hero earns them: 1 per fight, 2 per elite, 3 per boss.
long: Combat pays the party in talent points - every hero earns 1 for a fight, 2 for an elite, and 3 for a zone boss, spent on the Party screen. The FINAL boss pays no points; the relic it leaves behind is the prize. Rests, shops, and most events award none, so the fights you route through ARE your build budget.

short: Each zone boss grants some specs a whole new ability.
long: Felling a zone boss lets certain specs claim a trophy: one new ability chosen from their spec's pool on the Party screen. Today the Beastmaster, Sharpshooter, and Survivalist carry pools (five abilities each); other specs take the boss's relic and gold as their prize.

short: Every mini-boss hands each hero one: a permanent change to one ability.
long: Clearing a MINI-BOSS awards every hero an ability upgrade - a pick of three, resolved on that hero's map card. An upgrade is a permanent change to ONE ability the hero already owns, and it lasts the rest of the run. There are four: HONED (+50% damage), QUICKENED (-2 turns of cooldown, minimum 0), EFFORTLESS (costs no Rage / Mana / Focus - Mercy is unaffected), and SWIFT (arrives 25% sooner). Three mini-bosses a run means three upgrades per hero, twelve across the party. Upgrades STACK on a single ability - one ability can end a run Honed and Swift at once - but the SAME upgrade never comes twice to the same hero. They apply LAST, after talents and after equipped runes, so an upgrade always wins over a talent that sets the same field. You are only ever offered an upgrade that has something to change: Honed is never offered on a heal, Effortless never on a free ability. An upgraded ability wears a gold diamond on its button in battle and on its chip on the hero sheet; hovering it names the upgrades.

short: Every combat win makes the party permanently stronger this run.
long: Each battle won grants every hero +2% of their base Attack and HP for the rest of the run. Enemies climb their own ladder - roughly +2% Attack and +2.5% HP per tier, with a hard jump between zones - so a party that routes through more fights keeps pace; one that dodges them falls behind the curve.

short: This run's gear: slots grow each zone - 2, then 3, then 4.
long: Runes are equippable power for a single hero, found at the Peddler and in elite spoils (a pick of three). Slots grow with the run: 2 in the first zone, 3 in the second, 4 in the third. A rune's scope limits who can wear it - universal, one class, or one spec - and its rarity tells you its KIND, not just its size: common runes are flat stats, rares alter an ability you own or act like an extra talent, epics grant whole abilities or break a rule. Runes vanish with the run.

short: Crimson bargains: real power with a cost carved in.
long: A Scarred rune (crimson name) is a rare or epic with a drawback baked into it - more power than its clean cousin would dare, priced cheaper, and the cost is always written in the text. Read them twice; some scars are worth wearing.

short: Relics outlive the run; runes die with it.
long: The two are easy to confuse and could not be more different. RELICS are permanent: every zone boss you fell unlocks one FOREVER, and at the draft you choose up to 3 unlocked relics to carry - party-wide effects for the whole run. RUNES are of the run: bought and found along the way, worn by one hero, and gone the moment the run ends - by death or by victory. When you wipe, the relic you unlocked stays; the runes you were wearing do not.

short: The party's shared satchel, used in battle.
long: Five items, shared by the whole party and used in battle (press ALT or use the Items action): Health Potion (40 HP), Mana Potion (40 Mana or Rage), Bomb (50 damage to all enemies), Revive Potion (raise a fallen ally at 50% HP), and Defense Potion (+10% armor to the party, 3 turns). Loot nodes, shops, and elite spoils refill the satchel.

short: Three zones, each a 10-tier climb to its boss.
long: A run is three zones. Each zone is a map of 10 tiers - pick one node per tier, following the roads - with the zone boss waiting on top. Enemies grow with every tier and take a hard step up each zone; killing a boss fully restores the party, opens a new rune slot, and sends you down into the next zone. The third boss ends the run in victory.

short: Fights, elites, rests, shops, and mysteries - hover to scout.
long: Fight nodes are battles - hover one to scout its warband and what it resists. ELITE nodes are harder fights with the best rewards of the map. Rest nodes heal 30% HP and Mana. Shops sell consumables and a rune offer per hero. '???' events are unknown by design - no scout returns with the same story. Hovering any node tells you what it does before you commit; the roads out of your current node glow gold.

short: The map's hardest fights - and its best paydays.
long: From tier 6 up, some fights are ELITE: tougher warbands, often led by a chief. The payout is the run's snowball engine - 80-100 gold, 2 talent points per hero, a consumable, and a rune cache where one hero picks one of three runes. Routing through elites is how a strong party gets stronger; skipping them is how a weak one stays weak.

short: Three offers before every elite and mini-boss: a modifier plus a reward.
long: Before every ELITE and every MINI-BOSS - four a zone, and never before a plain fight or a boss - the road stops and offers three bargains. Each is one MODIFIER plus one REWARD, both shown before you choose. There is no decline: one of the three is taken. The modifier is the price and binds the coming battle only; the reward pays ON VICTORY, which is why 'a merchant follows the fight' is a reward you have to earn rather than a shop you walk into. Lose the fight and you paid the price for nothing. The offer screen shows the warband you are about to face and your party's health alongside the three cards, because choosing a severity-4 bargain at 30% health should be a decision, not a surprise.

short: A condition binding BOTH parties for one battle.
long: A modifier is a rule change that holds for exactly one battle and binds BOTH PARTIES - never just yours and never just theirs. Under Feverish everyone deals 25% more damage; under Bloodless nobody heals, on either side. That symmetry is the whole design: a modifier is a change to the fight, not a difficulty slider, so 'no items this fight' is not a modifier that exists because the enemy carries none. There are twenty, weighted toward the mild end because the safe slot on every bargain draws from that end and is therefore what you see most. The modifier is stamped on every combatant when the fight begins - a companion summoned mid-battle is bound by it too - and it is gone the moment the fight ends.

short: 1-4: how harsh a modifier is, and the only thing the reward reads.
long: Every modifier carries a severity of 1 to 4, shown as pips on its bargain card. The REWARD TABLE READS SEVERITY AND NOTHING ELSE: a 1 pays 40 gold, a 2 pays 80 gold or a potion, a 3 pays 140 gold or a rune, a 4 pays 220 gold, a rune, or a merchant after the fight. Severity is FLAT and deliberately ignores your party: a modifier that happens to be cheap for your build is a good deal you earned by building that way, and a severity that read the party would quietly tax every build for being good at something. EVERY OFFER HOLDS AT LEAST ONE OPTION OF SEVERITY 1 OR 2, guaranteed by how the cards are dealt rather than by luck, so a party on its last legs always has a survivable choice - and the other two cards are always 3s and 4s, so every bargain reads the same way: one safe option, two gambles.

short: Unknown by design: choices, bargains, and the occasional gift.
long: The violet '???' nodes are drawn at the door - not even scouting reveals them. Each offers choices, some gated by gold, party specs, or what the run has done so far. Events can wound the party but never kill anyone outright. Whether the road's strangers are worth trusting is yours to learn.

short: All four down ends the run - relics and the chronicle survive.
long: When the whole party falls, the run is over: gold, talents, runes, items, and the map are all lost. Two things survive every death - the RELICS you have unlocked (yours forever, pickable at the next draft) and the chronicle of cycles survived and lost. The run summary lays out how the attempt ended and what the party had built; the next climb starts wiser.

short: Standard, or the gentler Wanderer's road - chosen at the draft.
long: At the draft you choose the road: STANDARD is the game as designed; WANDERER softens every enemy to 70% of its strength. Wanderer exists so any tester can see all three zones and the finale - take it without shame, the game is being tuned and your eyes on the later zones are worth more than your pride.
